Services and searching

Source: vignettes/services-and-searching.Rmd
services-and-searching.Rmd
library(CDCLocator)

This article explains what cdc_providers() can search for and how a search works: the 14 services, the radius, how services combine, and why a search can take several requests.

The search 

cdc_providers(zipcode, radius = 10, services = NULL)
  • zipcode: a five-digit ZIP code as a string, such as "02110". The API searches around that ZIP code’s location. It doesn’t accept a city, an address or coordinates; to start from those, see “Searching from a place or a point” below.
  • radius: how far to search, in miles. A whole number from 1 to 50; the default is 10.
  • services: which kinds of provider to look for. NULL, the default, means all 14.

The 14 services

These are the values services accepts. Case doesn’t matter. The agency column says which federal program the listings come from, according to HIV.gov’s instructions for the API.

Value Covers Agency
hivtesting HIV testing CDC
stdtesting Testing for sexually transmitted infections CDC
selftesting Self-administered HIV and STI testing CDC
preptesting Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) providers CDC
pep Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) providers CDC
condom Free or low-cost condoms CDC
hepc Hepatitis C testing CDC
doxypep Doxycycline post-exposure prophylaxis (doxy-PEP) CDC
mailintesting Mail-in-only HIV self-testing kits CDC
ryanwhite Ryan White HIV/AIDS Program primary care, services and medications HRSA
clinics HRSA-funded health centers HRSA
substanceabuse State-licensed substance use disorder treatment SAMHSA
mentalhealth State-licensed mental health treatment SAMHSA
housing Help finding low-income affordable housing HUD

CDC is the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, HRSA the Health Resources and Services Administration, SAMHSA the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, and HUD the Department of Housing and Urban Development.

HIV.gov’s instructions spell hepatitis C as Hepc, but in November 2026 the API only matched hepc. The package sends every value in lower case, so either spelling works.

The public website at locator.hiv.gov shows some categories that aren’t on this list, such as tuberculosis testing. The API may not offer those.

How services combine

Naming several services finds providers that offer any of them, not all of them:

cdc_providers("20176", radius = 10, services = c("hivtesting", "stdtesting"))

returns everyone who offers HIV testing, plus everyone who offers STI testing.

To find providers that offer both, search for each and keep the ones that appear in both. Because the same clinic can have a different record for each service (see below), compare names and addresses rather than id:

hiv <- cdc_providers_tidy(
  cdc_providers("20176", radius = 10, services = "hivtesting")
)
sti <- cdc_providers_tidy(
  cdc_providers("20176", radius = 10, services = "stdtesting")
)
both <- merge(
  unique(hiv[, c("name", "street", "zipcode")]),
  unique(sti[, c("name", "street", "zipcode")])
)
both

Why a search can take several requests

When asked for all 14 services in one request, the API returned no providers at all, even where single-service searches found dozens. Requests with up to three services worked. So the package sends services three at a time and combines the answers:

Services asked for Requests
1 to 3 1
4 to 6 2
7 to 9 3
10 to 12 4
13 or 14 (the default) 5

Requests are spaced at least half a second apart, to go easy on the API, so the default search takes a few seconds. If you only need some services, naming them is faster.

If any of the requests fails, the whole search fails with that error. You never get a partial result without knowing it. (Searching several ZIP codes is different: see Searching many ZIP codes.)

Providers that come back from more than one request are kept once, matched by their id.

Duplicates across services

The API seems to keep a separate record for each service a place offers. In November 2026, searches for HIV testing and STI testing near the same ZIP code returned no shared ids, even though the same clinics appeared in both.

So when you search for several services, one clinic can appear several times, with different ids. vignette("working-with-results") shows how to collapse those rows by name and address when you want one row per place.

Searching from a place or a point

cdc_providers() only takes a ZIP code. Two functions translate other starting points:

cdc_address_place("Peoria", "IL")
cdc_address_point(40.69365, -89.58899)

cdc_address_place() takes a city and a state, written as the postal code ("IL") or in full. cdc_address_point() takes a latitude and longitude in decimal degrees; places in the US have negative longitudes. Both return the city, the full state name, the ZIP code and its coordinates.

Then search from that ZIP code:

place <- cdc_address_place("Peoria", "IL")
cdc_providers(place$zipcode, radius = 5, services = "ryanwhite")

The search is centered on the ZIP code, not on the exact point you started from, so distance in the results is measured from the ZIP code’s location.

Searching many ZIP codes

cdc_providers() also takes several ZIP codes. It searches around each in turn and combines the results:

zips <- c("20176", "20147", "20148")
nearby <- cdc_providers(zips, radius = 5, services = "hivtesting")
cdc_providers_tidy(nearby)

Some things to know:

  • Each provider is kept once. Nearby ZIP codes overlap, so the same record often comes back from more than one search. It is kept from the search where it was nearest, and search_zipcode says which one that was, so distance is measured from that ZIP code. To keep a row for every ZIP code that found a record, use distinct = FALSE; then the same provider can take several rows, so count providers with length(unique(nearby$id)), not nrow().
  • An unknown ZIP code is skipped, not fatal. If the API doesn’t know a ZIP code (“No point found for address”), the other searches carry on, and a warning at the end lists the ZIP codes skipped. The API’s messages are in attr(nearby, "failures"); read it straight away, because cdc_providers_tidy() and most data-frame operations drop it. Any other error, such as a refused request (HTTP 403) or a gateway error (502 or 504), stops the whole search, because it could hit every other ZIP code too. With a single ZIP code, every error stops the call, as before.
  • It takes time, on purpose. Requests are spaced at least one second apart when searching several ZIP codes, to go easy on the API: each ZIP code needs one request per three services, so 30 ZIP codes for every service is 150 requests, about two and a half minutes. Set min_gap to change the spacing (it can’t go below half a second). In an interactive session a progress bar shows how far the search has got, and a summary line follows at the end; progress = FALSE turns both off.
  • Stopping loses the results. Pressing Esc stops the search and discards what was found so far. For a long list, search it in smaller groups and combine them.
